params.why: angle B is a sensible triangle angle and leaves room for D and A
keeps angle A (equal to angle DEC) a plain acute or mildly obtuse angle

stem: In $\triangle ABD$, the point $C$ is the mid-point of $BD$ and the point $E$ is the mid-point of $AD$. Three angles are given: $\hat{D}={=d}^{\circ}$, $D\hat{E}C={=e}^{\circ}$ and $\hat{B}=({=p}x+{=c})^{\circ}$. Solve for the value of $x$.
solution: $C$ is the mid-point of $BD$ and $E$ is the mid-point of $AD$, so the line joining them is parallel to the third side: $AB \parallel EC$ (mid-point theorem).
$\hat{A}$ and $D\hat{E}C$ are corresponding angles, so $\hat{A}=D\hat{E}C={=e}^{\circ}$ (corresp $\angle$s; $AB \parallel EC$).
The angles of $\triangle ABD$ add up to $180^{\circ}$, so $\hat{B}=180^{\circ}-{=e}^{\circ}-{=d}^{\circ}={=bb}^{\circ}$ (sum of $\angle$s in a $\triangle$).
Both expressions are the size of $\hat{B}$, so ${=p}x+{=c}={=bb}$.
notes: Second advanced skeleton, the reverse order of smallexpr: the angle given in the small triangle (angle DEC) must first be carried to the big triangle by the mid-point theorem and corresponding angles (as in book ex7-8-21a with letters ABD, C, E), and only then used with the angle sum to reach the algebraic angle B. The algebraic-angle-in-an-equation twist comes from the book's ex7-7-15b and ex7-7-16b (page 268). No figure: the stem names every point and angle in words. Built backwards from x so x is a whole number; p is 2 to 6 so the coefficient never renders as 1x. Uses only the theorem direction and corresponding angles, as the book's solutions do; no lengths and no converse.
